summary.name: Geographic information system
summary.one_liner: Wikipedia article describing geographic information systems (GIS): computer systems and software for storing, managing, analyzing, and visualizing location-based data, along with their history and standards.
use_cases: understanding what a GIS is and how it works
researching the history of GIS and digital mapping
learning about raster versus vector spatial data
finding background on OGC geospatial standards
comparing commercial and open-source GIS software at a conceptual level
summary.what_it_does: The page is an encyclopedia overview of geographic information systems rather than a single downloadable tool. It defines GIS as hardware and software that store, manage, analyze, edit, output, and visualize geographic data, and uses location as the key index variable for relating information. It covers the history from 1832 cholera mapping and John Snow's 1854 map through Canada's CGIS in 1963 and early commercial products. It also describes data modeling (raster, vector, point clouds), data acquisition methods such as GPS, remote sensing and digitization, and the Open Geospatial Consortium standards. It names examples of GIS software including ArcGIS, QGIS, GRASS GIS, MapInfo Professional and GDAL-type libraries.
notable: Covers history from 1832 cholera mapping and 1854 John Snow map to modern GIS
Explains OGC open standards such as Web Map Service and OGC API - Features
Describes raster, vector and point cloud data models
Lists both commercial (ArcGIS, MapInfo) and open-source (QGIS, GRASS GIS) software
caveats: Encyclopedia article, not a software product; no download or pricing information
Page notes it needs more citations
